---
title: "Performance & Reliability"
---

IrisPipe is validated by three GitHub Actions workflows:

- **k6 Benchmark** measures runtime latency, API throughput, 1k / 10k / 100k data-volume behavior, failure semantics, and PostgreSQL → H2 JDBC coverage.
- **Backend K6 Checks** runs 10 regression suites against a real Spring Boot backend.
- **k6 Deep Volume Benchmark** runs scheduled/manual large-volume JOB / CHUNK benchmarks, including the 100k / 1M / 10M / 20M / 50M H2 ladder plus real relational-database coverage.

## What the Benchmark Measures

The benchmark workflows boot the real backend and execute `backend/k6/benchmark.js` and `backend/k6/data-volume-benchmark.js` against actual JDBC connections. They validate:

1. Synchronous pipeline execution latency plus API latency/request rate
2. H2 → H2 JOB vs CHUNK timing and rows/s at 1k / 10k / 100k in the regular benchmark gate
3. 10k failure semantics: JOB rolls back the whole job while CHUNK preserves previously committed chunks
4. PostgreSQL → H2 cross-database JDBC paths for both JOB and CHUNK
5. Scheduled/manual deep-volume runs at 100k / 1M / 10M / 20M / 50M for H2, with real RDBMS runs for PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, SQL Server, and Oracle at the sizes enabled by the deep matrix
6. External-destination row counts are verified after each real-RDBMS run, so a successful pipeline status alone is not accepted as a benchmark pass

All performance values are repeatable GitHub Actions CI-runner regression benchmarks, not production-capacity claims.

---

## JOB vs CHUNK: Transaction Boundary

The row count alone does not explain the atomicity trade-off. The benchmark deliberately records both **batch size** and **transaction groups**:

| CI profile | `fetchSize` / `batchSize` | JOB transaction boundary | CHUNK transaction boundary |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Regular PR/main benchmark | 1,000 rows | One destination transaction for the whole job | Commit every 1,000 rows |
| Scheduled/manual deep benchmark | 5,000 rows | One destination transaction for the whole job | Commit every 5,000 rows |

`fetchSize` / `batchSize` still controls JDBC read/write batching in JOB mode, but **does not split the transaction**. In CHUNK mode, the same batch size is also the commit/rollback boundary.

For the deep matrix, this means:

| Source rows | CHUNK transaction groups at 5,000 rows | JOB transaction groups |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 100k | 20 | 1 |
| 1M | 200 | 1 |
| 10M | 2,000 | 1 |
| 20M | 4,000 | 1 |
| 50M | 10,000 | 1 |

This is why both modes matter. **JOB** provides all-or-nothing rollback across the complete migration, but makes the transaction, rollback scope, and database resource pressure grow with the entire dataset. **CHUNK** bounds each transaction and retry scope, but a later failure preserves previously committed chunks and therefore requires explicit resume/recovery semantics.

The regular 10k failure test makes that difference observable. It injects a duplicate key on the final source row with a 1,000-row batch: JOB rolls back all migrated rows and leaves only the pre-existing conflicting row (**1 row**); CHUNK keeps the first nine committed chunks (**9,000 rows**) and rolls back the failing tenth chunk, so together with the pre-existing conflict row the destination contains **9,001 rows**.

## Test Strategy

k6 is used for **integration-level correctness**, not only synthetic load generation.
Each regression suite:

1. Boots the real Spring Boot backend from a compiled jar
2. Runs API flows that exercise a specific behavioral domain
3. Asserts on status codes, response shape, persisted state, and runtime transitions
4. Tears down cleanly

The deep benchmark additionally starts the target database in CI, seeds the source set inside that database, executes IrisPipe through JDBC, and verifies the destination row count from the database itself.

This exercises the stack end-to-end: controller → service → Spring Batch → JDBC driver → database.

## CI Pipeline

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
  P["PR / push"] --> B["mvn package + unit tests"]
  B --> A["API / runtime benchmark"]
  B --> V["Regular data-volume\nJOB / CHUNK × 1k / 10k / 100k"]
  B --> F["10k failure semantics\nJOB / CHUNK"]
  B --> X["PostgreSQL → H2\nJOB / CHUNK"]
  B --> R["10-suite k6 regression matrix"]

  S["Scheduled / manual deep run"] --> DB["Real DB containers + in-DB seed"]
  DB --> H["H2 ladder\n100k / 1M / 10M / 20M / 50M"]
  DB --> M["RDBMS matrix\nPostgreSQL / MySQL / MariaDB / SQL Server / Oracle"]
  H --> DP["Verify destination + deep-performance-results.json"]
  M --> DP

  A --> KP["performance-results.json"]
  V --> KP
  F --> KP
  X --> KP
  R --> RP["k6-regression-results.json"]

  KP --> Q["Render Quarto site"]
  RP --> Q
  DP --> Q
  Q --> D["Deploy GitHub Pages"]
```

## Benchmark Methodology

The benchmark workflows:

1. Run `mvn package`, so backend unit tests are part of the gate
2. Build one runnable jar and reuse it across benchmark jobs
3. Keep the regular PR/main benchmark bounded to API/runtime, 1k / 10k / 100k H2 volume, 10k failure semantics, and PostgreSQL → H2 coverage
4. Keep 10M+ capacity work out of normal PR latency by using a scheduled/manual deep workflow
5. Run the H2 deep ladder at 100k / 1M / 10M / 20M / 50M for both JOB and CHUNK
6. Start real PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, SQL Server, and Oracle instances for deep JDBC verification; source data is generated inside the database rather than sent row-by-row through k6
7. Verify the external destination row count after the pipeline completes and mark the report failed if the count differs
8. Aggregate JSON artifacts into Quarto result files and deploy GitHub Pages
